# Maze game (9 levels)

## Rendering model
- Board is a node graph drawn on 24px cells. Node cells sit on a lattice spaced 48px
  (node top-left at x=X0+48c, y=Y0+48r). A 24px GRAY (#999999) cell between two nodes
  means those nodes are connected (open corridor). Black = nothing.
- Colors: white #FFFFFF = normal node, blue #1E93FF = player (has dark #333333 marker
  showing last-move direction), green #4FCC30 = goal, red #F93C31 = special node
  (level 2 has one with a purple #A356D6 center), gray = corridor.
- Bottom pink strip = per-level move/step meter; it fills (turns white) as moves are used.
  It reset to full pink at the new level.

## Controls
- ACTION1=up, ACTION2=down, ACTION3=left, ACTION4=right. Each action moves the player
  exactly one node along an open corridor. Blocked moves presumably do nothing.
- Reaching green completes the level (progress +1) and immediately loads the next maze
  in the same session (no RESET needed).

## Method that works
1. read_pixels over the drawn area with 8px bins (3 bins per 24px cell) to recover the
   node lattice and which connectors are gray.
2. Build adjacency, BFS shortest path player->goal, then issue that move sequence.

## Progress
- Level 1 solved in 18 moves (6x6 lattice, single forced path).

# Maze game (9 levels)

## Rendering model
- Node graph on a 24px cell grid; nodes sit on a 48px lattice (node top-left x=X0+48c,
  y=Y0+48r, X0~88/96). A 24px GRAY (#999999) cell between two nodes = open corridor.
  Black = nothing.
- Colors: white #FFFFFF normal node, blue #1E93FF player (dark #333333 marker on the face
  it last moved toward), green #4FCC30 goal, red #F93C31 guard with a purple #A356D6
  marker on ONE face = the direction it faces, gray = corridor.
- Bottom pink strip = per-level move meter; fills white from the right as moves are used.

## Controls
- ACTION1=up, ACTION2=down, ACTION3=left, ACTION4=right; one node per action along an
  open corridor. Reaching green completes the level and immediately loads the next.

## Red guard mechanic (learned in level 2)
- A guard is STATIONARY. It ignores the player at any distance, even adjacent.
- If the player steps into the single cell the guard FACES (purple marker side), the guard
  immediately lunges one step in that direction onto the player => GAME_OVER.
- Moving INTO the guard's cell from any other side DESTROYS the guard; the player takes
  its cell. This is how you clear a guard blocking a corridor.
- So: never enter the faced cell; attack the guard from its back/side instead.

## Method
1. read_pixels with 8px bins over the drawn area to recover nodes/corridors and the
   positions + facings of player, goal, guards.
2. BFS shortest path, excluding each guard's faced cell as a forbidden node; guard cells
   themselves are enterable (from a non-faced side) and clear the guard.

## Progress
- L1 solved (18 moves). L2 solved (10 moves after 1 death that taught the guard rule).

# Maze game (9 levels)

## Rendering model
- Node graph on 24px cells; nodes on a 48px lattice, with a 24px GRAY (#999999) cell
  between two nodes meaning an open corridor. Black = nothing. Grid origin varies per
  level but is always a multiple of 8 (usually of 24).
- Colors: white #FFFFFF node, blue #1E93FF player (dark #333333 marker = last move dir),
  green #4FCC30 goal, red #F93C31 static guard, orange #FF851B moving guard, purple
  #A356D6 marker = the face/direction that guard is pointed at.
- Bottom pink strip = per-level move meter, fills white from the right as moves are used
  (~2% per move; budget is generous, ~50 moves).

## Controls
- ACTION1 up, ACTION2 down, ACTION3 left, ACTION4 right: one node per action.
  Reaching green completes the level and immediately loads the next.

## Guard mechanics (verified L2-L4)
- RED guard: never moves on its own. If the player steps into the one cell it faces,
  it lunges there and kills => that cell is permanently forbidden while it lives.
- ORANGE guard: patrols its corridor, moving exactly one cell per player action in the
  direction it faces; at the end of the corridor its marker flips and it comes back
  (deterministic, so its position can be simulated turn by turn). It kills by moving
  onto the player, so never end a move on the cell it will step into.
- BOTH: moving INTO a guard's cell from any side other than its faced side destroys it
  and the player takes that cell. This is the standard way to clear a blocker.

## Method
1. read_pixels with 8px bins over the drawn area (3 bins per 24px cell) to recover nodes,
   corridors, player/goal and every guard cell + purple marker face.
2. Simulate orange guards' positions per turn; BFS shortest path treating red faced cells
   as forbidden and timing moves so the player never occupies an orange's next cell.
   Waiting is impossible - burn time by stepping back and forth in a safe side corridor.

## Progress
- L1 18 moves; L2 10 (1 death); L3 19; L4 17. Now L5 (4/9 done).

# Level 5 (progress 4/9) - TIMED PLAN

Grid: C0..C7 x=72+48c; R0..R5 y=112+48r. Player start (R0,C7) at t=0.
Player parity: at time t the player cell has (r+c) parity = (7+t) mod 2.
Move meter ~42 moves for this level (12px per move of 512).

Patrol models (t = my move count; verified through t=2):
- O1 & O4 in column C3, rows 0..5. O1 row = f(t), O4 row = f(t+4), f by t mod 10:
  t%10: 0->2 1->3 2->4 3->5 4->4 5->3 6->2 7->1 8->0 9->1
  => C3 rows occupied by t%10: 0:{2,4} 1:{3} 2:{2,4} 3:{1,5} 4:{0,4} 5:{1,3} 6:{2} 7:{1,3} 8:{0,4} 9:{1,5}
- O2 patrols row R3 C0..C7, period 14: t%14: 0:C0 1:C1 2:C2 3:C3 4:C4 5:C5 6:C6 7:C7
  8:C6 9:C5 10:C4 11:C3 12:C2 13:C1
- O3 patrols column C2 rows R2..R4: at (R3,C2) at EVERY EVEN t (=> (R3,C2) is
  permanently unusable for me, my parity there is even), (R4,C2) at t%4==1, (R2,C2) at t%4==3.

Consequence: goal (R3,C3) reachable only from (R3,C4), at odd T with T%10 in {3,9},
T%14 not in {3,11,4}. Earliest feasible T = 29.

# Maze game (9 levels)

## Rendering model
- Node graph on 24px cells; nodes on a 48px lattice, a 24px GRAY (#999999) cell between
  two nodes = open corridor. Black = nothing. Grid origin varies per level (multiple of 8).
- Colors: white #FFFFFF node, blue #1E93FF player (dark marker = last move dir), green
  #4FCC30 goal, red #F93C31 static guard, dark red #921231 hunter guard, orange #FF851B
  patrolling guard, purple #A356D6 marker = the face the guard is pointed at,
  yellow #FFDC00 marker = that guard is in attack/pursuit mode.
- Bottom pink strip (y~500) = move meter, drains left-to-right; rate varies per level
  (8-12px per move of 512 => ~40-64 moves budget). Measure it when planning long routes.

## Controls
- ACTION1 up, ACTION2 down, ACTION3 left, ACTION4 right: one node per action.
  Reaching green completes the level and immediately loads the next. No wait action:
  burn time by stepping back and forth.

## Guard mechanics (verified L2-L7)
- RED (static): never moves. Stepping into the single cell it FACES = it lunges there and
  kills you. That faced cell is forbidden while it lives.
- ORANGE (patroller): moves one cell per player action along its corridor in its facing
  direction; flips at the corridor end (deterministic, simulate it). Kills by moving onto
  the player. Guards/patrollers pass through and stack on each other harmlessly.
- DARK RED (hunter): starts static like a red. If the player steps anywhere into its
  line/corridor it turns yellow and pursues one cell per player action, turning corners to
  follow the player. It kills only by reaching the player's cell, so staying >=2 cells
  ahead and never doubling back keeps you safe.
- ALL guards: moving INTO a guard's cell from any side other than its faced side destroys
  it and the player takes the cell. Standard way to clear blockers.

## Method
1. read_pixels with 8px bins over the drawn area (3 bins per 24px cell) to recover nodes,
   corridors, player/goal, every guard cell and its purple marker face.
2. Note the player's parity: cell (r+c) parity flips every move, so some cells are only
   reachable on even/odd turns - combined with a patroller's period this can make a cell
   permanently unusable (happened in L5 and L6).
3. BFS with time: forbid red faced cells, simulate orange positions per turn (avoid both
   sharing a cell and swapping), and plan kill order for chained guards.

## Progress

- ACTION1/2/3/4 = up/down/left/right, one node per action; no wait action (burn time by
  stepping back and forth, but only where safe). Reaching green ends the level instantly.

## Guard rules (all verified)
- RED (static): never moves; kills anyone standing on the single cell it faces.
- ORANGE (patroller): moves one cell per player action along its corridor, flipping at
  each end (fully deterministic: tabulate position by t mod period). Kills by moving onto
  the player. Guards pass through/stack on each other harmlessly.
- DARK RED (hunter): static until the player enters its faced line (range >= 2); then it
  turns yellow and pursues one cell per action FOREVER, staying exactly 2 behind.
  Crucially it follows the player's TRAIL (its move targets the player's previous cell),
  so it never cuts corners to capture - a route that never doubles back is always safe.
- ANY guard, moving or static, is DESTROYED by moving into its cell from a side other
  than the one it faces; the player takes the cell. This is the main tool for opening
  blocked corridors (and for deleting patrollers that are in the way).

   reachable on even or odd turns. Combined with a patroller's period this can make a
   cell permanently unreachable (L5, L6) - check this before assuming a route exists.
3. Time-indexed BFS: forbid red faced cells, simulate every patroller per turn, avoid
   both sharing a cell and swapping through one, and order guard kills by dependency
   (a guard can only be rammed from a side that is itself safe to stand on).
4. With a hunter active, the route must be a simple non-backtracking path; laps around
   6-cycles are safe for burning time, 4-cycles are not (the pursuer ends up adjacent).

- **L1–L2:** Learned the board is a 48px node lattice with gray corridors, and paid for the one death of the run to discover the red guard rule: a static guard kills you only on the single cell its purple marker faces — and you destroy it by ramming it from any other side.
- **L3–L4:** Chained guard kills in dependency order, and met the orange patroller (one cell per action, flips at corridor ends) — simulated its cycle and slipped in behind it.
- **L5–L6:** The big insight was **parity**: the player's cell colour alternates every move, so a patroller with the right period can make a cell permanently unreachable. That ruled out the "obvious" routes and forced long timed detours (29 and 30 moves) which I verified against the patrol tables every single turn.
- **L7–L8:** The dark-red **hunter** appeared — it triggers on line of sight, then pursues one cell per action forever. Key discovery: it stays exactly 2 behind and follows your trail, so a never-doubling-back route (and a 6-cycle lap to bait it off its post) beats it.
- **L9:** Everything at once — three patrollers, a hunter triggered on move 1, and two reds guarding the goal cell itself. I lapped the safe 6-cycle twice to phase-align with the patrollers, killed a patroller by ramming it perpendicular (new: moving guards can be destroyed too), threaded the column dodge on the one turn the hunter's trail-following behaviour made survivable, then cleared both reds from their blind sides before stepping onto the goal.

GUIDE.md now holds the complete, verified model: rendering, the three guard behaviours, the ram rule, the parity check, and the time-indexed planning method.
